north-carolina-coast-sandy-inlet-dunes-s.head: After Charleston, Blackbeard sailed north to the coast of North Carolina.
north-carolina-coast-sandy-inlet-dunes-s.body: The coast of North Carolina is very different from the Caribbean. It is lined by the Outer Banks, a chain of long, narrow sandy islands stretching for about two hundred miles. Behind them lie wide, shallow lagoons called sounds, such as Pamlico Sound and Albemarle Sound. Narrow channels, called inlets, connect the sounds with the ocean. These inlets shift constantly as storms move the sand. In 1718, the coast was sparsely settled. Historians note that the shallow waters and shifting channels made the area difficult for large ships, but suitable for small sloops that knew the way. This made the coast attractive to pirates. Few officials lived there, and the colony's government was weak. In early June 1718, Blackbeard's fleet approached an inlet called Topsail Inlet, today known as Beaufort Inlet. Even so, the shallow entrance was risky for a large ship like the Queen Anne's Revenge. What happened next changed the course of Blackbeard's career.

large-ship-aground-sandbar-inlet-tilted-.head: In June 1718, the Queen Anne's Revenge ran aground at Topsail Inlet, now Beaufort Inlet, and was lost.
large-ship-aground-sandbar-inlet-tilted-.body: As the Queen Anne's Revenge entered Topsail Inlet, she struck a sandbar and stuck fast. One of the smaller ships, the sloop Adventure, commanded by Israel Hands, tried to help pull her free. The Adventure also ran aground and was wrecked. Historians have long debated whether this was an accident. Some members of the crew later claimed that Blackbeard ran the ships aground deliberately. According to this view, his fleet had become too large, with too many men expecting a share of the loot. By losing the big ship, he could reduce the crew and keep more for himself and his closest companions. Testimony from a crew member named David Herriot supports this interpretation. Even so, it is impossible to know for certain. The inlet was difficult, and accidents were common. Whatever the cause, the loss of the Queen Anne's Revenge marked the end of Blackbeard's great fleet.

sailors-unloading-boats-sandy-shore-inle.head: After the wreck, Blackbeard left many of his crew behind and sailed away with the most valuable goods.
sailors-unloading-boats-sandy-shore-inle.body: After the ships ran aground, Blackbeard acted quickly. He sent Stede Bonnet to the town of Bath to ask the governor of North Carolina for a royal pardon. While Bonnet was away, Blackbeard transferred the most valuable goods from the wrecks to a smaller sloop. He then sailed off with a small group of trusted men. Many others were left stranded on a sandy island, according to later testimony. When Bonnet returned, he rescued some of the stranded men. Historians use the accounts of crew members, given during later trials, to reconstruct these events. These accounts suggest that Blackbeard deliberately broke up his crew. Even so, the testimonies were given by men trying to save their own lives, so they may not be fully reliable. The episode shows that pirate loyalty had limits. Blackbeard, like other captains, made decisions that served his own interests, even at the expense of his crew.

bath-north-carolina-1718-small-village-c.head: In June 1718, Blackbeard accepted a royal pardon from the governor of North Carolina at Bath.
bath-north-carolina-1718-small-village-c.body: In September 1717, King George the First issued a proclamation offering a pardon to any pirate who surrendered to a colonial governor before a set date in 1718. Pirates who accepted it would be forgiven for past crimes if they gave up piracy. Many pirates accepted, including Benjamin Hornigold. In June 1718, Blackbeard sailed to Bath, the oldest town in North Carolina, founded in 1705. There, he received a pardon from Governor Charles Eden. Bath was a small settlement on a creek off the Pamlico River, with a few dozen houses, a courthouse and a church under construction. Historians have debated the relationship between Blackbeard and Governor Eden. Some suspected that Eden and his secretary, Tobias Knight, cooperated with Blackbeard in exchange for goods. Even so, the evidence is unclear. A later investigation cleared Eden of wrongdoing, though suspicions about Knight remained. For a time, Blackbeard lived in or near Bath as a pardoned man.

creek-side-house-garden-oaks-summer-even.head: Local stories about Blackbeard's house and treasure at Bath cannot be confirmed.
creek-side-house-garden-oaks-summer-even.body: People in Bath still tell stories about Blackbeard. Some say he lived in a house on Plum Point, a point of land near the mouth of Bath Creek. Others say tunnels connected his house to the governor's. There are also stories of hidden treasure. Historians have found no evidence to support these tales. They appear to have developed over generations of local storytelling. Even so, Blackbeard clearly spent time in the area during the summer of 1718. He did not remain peaceful for long. Within a few months, he returned to sea. Near Bermuda, he captured two French ships loaded with sugar and cocoa. He brought one of them back to North Carolina and claimed that he had found it abandoned at sea. The local court accepted this story and allowed him to keep the cargo. Historians see this as further evidence that some officials in the colony were willing to overlook his activities.

ocracoke-island-sound-side-live-oaks-slo.head: Blackbeard used Ocracoke Island, on the Outer Banks, as his base in the autumn of 1718.
ocracoke-island-sound-side-live-oaks-slo.body: Ocracoke is an island near the southern end of the Outer Banks. Next to it lies Ocracoke Inlet, one of the most important channels between the ocean and Pamlico Sound in the eighteenth century. Ships bound for the towns of North Carolina passed through it. From Ocracoke, Blackbeard could watch traffic in and out of the sound. He anchored his sloop in a deep channel on the sound side of the island, near the southern tip. This place is still known as Teach's Hole. In October 1718, another famous pirate, Charles Vane, visited Blackbeard at Ocracoke. Vane had refused the pardon and escaped from Nassau. According to reports, the two crews held a large gathering on the island, with drinking and celebration. Historians know of this meeting from later testimony and from alarmed reports by officials. Even so, details of the gathering are uncertain. It raised fears that Ocracoke might become a new pirate base like Nassau.

governor-spotswood-williamsburg-palace-o.head: Governor Alexander Spotswood of Virginia secretly planned an expedition to capture Blackbeard.
governor-spotswood-williamsburg-palace-o.body: Alexander Spotswood was the lieutenant governor of Virginia, the neighbouring colony to the north. He was an energetic and ambitious administrator. Spotswood was alarmed by reports of pirates gathering at Ocracoke. He did not trust the government of North Carolina to deal with them, suspecting that some officials there protected Blackbeard. Legally, Spotswood had no authority to send an expedition into another colony. Even so, he decided to act. In November 1718, he secretly organised a mission to find and capture Blackbeard. He also issued a proclamation offering rewards for the capture or death of pirates. Historians know about his plans from his own letters to London, which survive in British archives. Spotswood defended his actions as necessary to protect trade. Yet his decision was controversial. It later caused disputes with the government of North Carolina. Spotswood's residence in Williamsburg, the Governor's Palace, has been reconstructed and is now part of Colonial Williamsburg.

colonial-farmhouse-north-carolina-1718-t.head: In 1718, North Carolina was a poor and thinly settled colony of small farms.
colonial-farmhouse-north-carolina-1718-t.body: North Carolina was one of the least developed English colonies in America. Its population in 1718 was perhaps around twenty thousand settlers, together with enslaved Africans and Native American communities. Most colonists lived on small farms along rivers and sounds. They grew tobacco, corn and vegetables, raised pigs and cattle, and produced tar, pitch and turpentine from pine forests. Roads were few, and travel was mostly by boat. Historians note that the shallow coast and lack of good harbours made trade difficult. Much of the colony's produce passed through Virginia. Even so, land was available, and many settlers valued their independence. There were few towns, schools or churches. Courts and government were weak. Historians describe North Carolina at this time as a place where people were used to managing their own affairs and were often suspicious of authority. This environment helped make the colony a convenient place for pirates.

log-house-porch-brick-chimney-children-c.head: Ordinary settlers in North Carolina lived simple lives in log or timber houses.
log-house-porch-brick-chimney-children-c.body: A typical settler family in North Carolina in 1718 lived in a small house built of logs or timber, often with a single room and a loft. A chimney of brick or clay stood at one end. Families raised chickens and pigs in the yard and grew vegetables in a garden. Life was hard and often lonely. Doctors, schools and churches were few and far apart. Historians know about daily life in the colony from court records, wills, inventories and the reports of missionaries. Some colonists traded with passing ships and did not ask too many questions about where goods came from. Pirates could sell cloth, sugar and tools cheaply. This made them welcome to some settlers, who had little access to imported goods. Even so, others feared and disliked them. Settlers knew that pirates could be dangerous. Some had suffered from raids and robberies along the coast. Attitudes toward Blackbeard in the colony were therefore mixed.

small-colonial-wharf-trading-sloop-barre.head: North Carolina had recently suffered the Tuscarora War, which left much of the colony poor and unsettled.
small-colonial-wharf-trading-sloop-barre.body: From 1711 to 1715, the colony of North Carolina was involved in a bitter conflict with the Tuscarora people. The Tuscarora were a powerful Native nation whose lands settlers had steadily occupied. In September 1711, Tuscarora warriors attacked settlements along the rivers, killing many colonists. The colony requested help from South Carolina and Virginia. Expeditions supported by Native allies defeated the Tuscarora in the following years. Many Tuscarora were killed or enslaved, and many others moved north to join the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois Confederacy, in New York. Historians note that the war left North Carolina weakened, with damaged farms and a struggling economy. Even so, by 1718 settlement was expanding again. The colony's weakness helped explain why it had little power to stop pirates. Trade with pirates offered some colonists goods they could not otherwise afford, which made enforcement even more difficult for the authorities.

outer-banks-fisherman-small-boat-nets-so.head: People living on the Outer Banks fished, raised livestock and watched ships passing along the coast.
outer-banks-fisherman-small-boat-nets-so.body: In the early eighteenth century, only a few people lived on the Outer Banks. They fished in the sounds, raised cattle and horses on the islands and salvaged goods from shipwrecks. They knew the channels and sandbars well. Some acted as pilots, guiding ships through the dangerous inlets. Historians note that wrecks were frequent along this coast, which later became known as the Graveyard of the Atlantic. Islanders saw many ships pass. In the summer and autumn of 1718, among them was a sloop commanded by a captain with a long black beard. Local traditions about Blackbeard developed among these communities and were passed down through generations. Even so, few written records survive from islanders of this period. Most of what historians know comes from colonial officials, court records and later accounts. The Outer Banks remained a remote and quiet place for many generations, shaped by the sea and by isolation.

navy-warships-entering-nassau-harbour-ju.head: In July 1718, Woodes Rogers arrived in Nassau as the new governor of the Bahamas.
navy-warships-entering-nassau-harbour-ju.body: British authorities decided to restore control over the Bahamas. They appointed Woodes Rogers as governor. Rogers was a former privateer captain from Bristol. Between 1708 and 1711, he had led a famous voyage around the world, during which his crew rescued Alexander Selkirk, a castaway whose story later inspired the novel Robinson Crusoe. In July 1718, Rogers arrived at Nassau with warships, soldiers and settlers. He announced the king's pardon to the pirates. Many accepted it. One pirate captain, Charles Vane, refused. He set a captured ship on fire and sent it toward the warships, then escaped through another channel. Historians know about these events from Rogers' own reports and other accounts. Even so, the pardon did not end piracy immediately. Some pardoned men soon returned to their old ways. Rogers faced a difficult task, governing a lawless town with few resources and many former pirates.

sloop-escaping-harbour-dawn-warships-beh.head: Woodes Rogers gradually restored order in Nassau and made it a working colony again.
sloop-escaping-harbour-dawn-warships-beh.body: After his arrival, Woodes Rogers repaired the fort, organised a militia and encouraged settlers to clear land and plant crops. The work was difficult. Many of the newly arrived settlers fell ill with fevers, and some died. Supplies were short, and help from Britain was limited. Some pardoned pirates returned to piracy. In December 1718, Rogers held a trial of pirates who had broken the pardon, and eight were hanged in Nassau. Historians see this as a turning point in ending the pirate republic. Benjamin Hornigold, Blackbeard's former captain, helped Rogers by hunting down pirates. Even so, Rogers struggled financially and was later imprisoned for debt in England. He returned to the Bahamas as governor in 1729 and died there in 1732. The motto of the Bahamas for many years, Expulsis Piratis, Restituta Commercia, meaning pirates expelled, commerce restored, reflects his achievement.

colonial-fort-nassau-repair-workers-ston.head: By the autumn of 1718, the golden age of piracy was beginning to decline.
colonial-fort-nassau-repair-workers-ston.body: The pirates had lost their main base at Nassau. The royal pardon had persuaded many to give up piracy. The Royal Navy was sending more warships to American waters. Colonies were organising their own expeditions against pirates. Historians note that between 1716 and 1726, hundreds of pirates were hanged in the Atlantic world. Several famous pirates met their end around this time. Samuel Bellamy, known as Black Sam, had drowned in April 1717 when his ship, the Whydah, was wrecked off Cape Cod in a storm. The wreck of the Whydah was discovered in 1984 and is the first confirmed pirate shipwreck ever found. Charles Vane was later captured and hanged in Jamaica in 1721. John Rackham, known as Calico Jack, was captured in 1720 with the famous women pirates Anne Bonny and Mary Read. Even so, piracy did not disappear at once. It continued in decreasing numbers until the late 1720s.

two-small-sloops-sailing-calm-sound-nove.head: In November 1718, two small sloops sailed from Virginia toward Ocracoke under Lieutenant Robert Maynard.
two-small-sloops-sailing-calm-sound-nove.body: Governor Spotswood hired two small sloops, named the Jane and the Ranger, for his expedition. Large navy warships could not enter the shallow waters of the sounds, so smaller vessels were needed. The sloops carried no cannons. On board were about sixty sailors from two Royal Navy ships, HMS Pearl and HMS Lyme, which were stationed in Virginia. They were commanded by Lieutenant Robert Maynard of HMS Pearl. At the same time, Spotswood sent a force overland toward Bath. Historians know about the expedition from Maynard's own report and Spotswood's letters. The sloops reached Ocracoke on the evening of the twenty-first of November 1718. They found Blackbeard's sloop, the Adventure, anchored near the southern end of the island. Blackbeard had only about twenty men with him at the time. Even so, he was experienced and well armed. Maynard decided to wait until morning before approaching through the shallow channels.

evening-sound-anchored-sloops-lanterns-q.head: On the twenty-second of November 1718, Blackbeard was killed in a short battle at Ocracoke.
evening-sound-anchored-sloops-lanterns-q.body: Maynard did not attack at night because the channels were narrow and full of sandbars that he did not know. The two sides waited through the night, a short distance apart. At dawn on the twenty-second of November, Maynard's sloops moved toward Blackbeard's ship. Both of Maynard's sloops ran aground on sandbars as they approached. Blackbeard's crew fired their cannons, causing many casualties. Maynard then ordered most of his men to hide below deck. When Blackbeard's men boarded Maynard's sloop, the hidden sailors rushed up to fight. In a fierce but short struggle, Blackbeard was killed. According to Maynard's report, he had received many wounds. Several other pirates died, and the rest surrendered. Historians rely mainly on Maynard's report and on later accounts, which differ in some details. Even so, the main events are clear. The most famous pirate of his age died not in a great sea battle, but in a brief fight in a quiet sound.

ocracoke-sound-calm-morning-after-gulls-.head: Blackbeard's surviving crew were tried in Williamsburg, Virginia, in March 1719.
ocracoke-sound-calm-morning-after-gulls-.body: After the battle, Maynard sailed to Bath and then back to Virginia with his prisoners. The captured pirates, together with others arrested in North Carolina, were taken to Williamsburg, the capital of Virginia. Their trial took place in March 1719. Most were found guilty and hanged. One man, Samuel Odell, was acquitted. He had been a trader who happened to be aboard Blackbeard's sloop the night before the battle. Israel Hands, Blackbeard's former sailing master, had not been present at Ocracoke. He gave evidence against others, received a pardon and, according to Johnson, later lived as a beggar in London. Historians use the surviving trial records and Spotswood's letters to understand these events. Even so, the full records of the trial have not survived. The case also led to a long dispute between Virginia and North Carolina, because Spotswood had acted in another colony without permission.

quiet-colonial-church-graveyard-oaks-bat.head: Blackbeard was a pirate for only about two years, yet he became the most famous pirate in history.
quiet-colonial-church-graveyard-oaks-bat.body: Blackbeard's career as a pirate lasted roughly from 1716 to 1718. In that short time, he captured dozens of ships, blockaded Charleston and commanded one of the most powerful pirate fleets ever seen in the Americas. Historians note that his fame owed much to his deliberate use of reputation and appearance, and to Johnson's book, which made him the central character of pirate history. In Bath, the Church of Saint Thomas, begun in 1734, is the oldest existing church in North Carolina. It stands among old oaks, close to the waters Blackbeard once sailed. The town remains small and quiet, with historic houses and gardens. Even so, Blackbeard's story was quickly turned into legend. Within a few years of his death, he had become a symbol of pirate life. His real life, as recorded in documents, is less dramatic than the legend, but in many ways more interesting and more human.

old-book-general-history-pyrates-1724-en.head: The golden age of piracy ended in the 1720s, after navies and colonies acted against pirates.
old-book-general-history-pyrates-1724-en.body: After Blackbeard's death, piracy continued for several more years, but on a smaller scale. Navies of Britain, France and Spain sent more warships to American waters. Colonies passed stricter laws and held more trials. Bartholomew Roberts, perhaps the most successful pirate of the period, captured hundreds of ships before he was killed in battle off West Africa in 1722. After his death, more than fifty of his crew were hanged. Historians generally date the end of the golden age of piracy to about 1726. In 1724, Johnson's book was published in London. It became very popular and was reprinted and translated many times. It shaped how people imagined pirates for centuries. Even so, historians note that Johnson mixed fact with fiction. Some chapters, such as those about certain pirates, may be largely invented. Yet the book remains an important source, because it preserved information from trials and newspapers that has otherwise been lost.

one-legged-sailor-parrot-shoulder-ship-g.head: Robert Louis Stevenson's novel Treasure Island, published in 1883, created many of the most familiar pirate images.
one-legged-sailor-parrot-shoulder-ship-g.body: Many popular ideas about pirates come from a single novel. Treasure Island was written by the Scottish author Robert Louis Stevenson and published as a book in 1883. It tells the story of a boy, Jim Hawkins, who joins a voyage to find buried treasure. The book introduced or popularised treasure maps marked with an X, buried treasure on islands, a parrot that cries pieces of eight, and the one-legged pirate Long John Silver. It also included the song about fifteen men on the dead man's chest. Stevenson used real history in places. He mentioned Blackbeard and named one of his characters Israel Hands, after Blackbeard's real sailing master. Historians note that the novel drew on Johnson's book. Even so, most of the story was invented. Treasure Island became one of the most famous adventure stories in the world. It has inspired countless films, plays and books, and continues to shape how pirates are imagined today.

theatre-stage-pirate-ship-painted-scener.head: Walking the plank and buried treasure were very rare or unknown among real pirates.
theatre-stage-pirate-ship-painted-scener.body: Pirates appear in many plays, films and books, often with sword fights, treasure and dramatic punishments. Walking the plank is one of the best-known pirate images. Historians have found almost no evidence that pirates of Blackbeard's time made prisoners walk the plank. A few later reports exist, mainly from the nineteenth century, but the practice was very rare. Buried treasure is also mostly a myth. One famous exception is the privateer William Kidd, who buried some valuables on Gardiners Island, near New York, in 1699, before he was arrested. The treasure was recovered by the authorities soon afterwards. Historians note that Kidd's story helped create the legend of buried pirate gold. Even so, most pirates had no reason to bury anything. Their loot was usually goods, not coins, and they spent what they gained quickly. Popular entertainment has made pirates more colourful and dramatic than the records suggest.

pirate-ship-sunset-calm-sea-crew-silhoue.head: Most real pirates did not become rich and did not live long.
pirate-ship-sunset-calm-sea-crew-silhoue.body: Historians who study trial records and shipping documents have found that the lives of most pirates were short and difficult. Many died of disease, drowned in wrecks or were killed in fights. Hundreds were hanged. Few managed to retire with their gains. Most of what they captured was spent quickly. Historians such as Marcus Rediker estimate that between about 1716 and 1726, several thousand men took part in piracy in the Atlantic. Some accepted pardons and returned to ordinary lives as sailors or settlers. Their later lives are mostly unknown. Even so, for a few years, pirates challenged the power of empires and the trade on which those empires depended. Their stories were told in newspapers, trials and books, and later in novels and films. Unlike Blackbeard, most of them were soon forgotten. Their names survive only in a few documents, quietly preserved in archives on both sides of the Atlantic.

research-boat-beaufort-inlet-divers-calm.head: The wreck of the Queen Anne's Revenge was discovered in Beaufort Inlet in 1996.
research-boat-beaufort-inlet-divers-calm.body: For almost three hundred years, nobody knew exactly where the Queen Anne's Revenge lay. People knew that she had run aground at Topsail Inlet, now called Beaufort Inlet, in North Carolina. But the inlet had changed many times as storms moved the sand. In November 1996, a team from a private research company, Intersal, found a wreck in about twenty feet of water near the inlet. They found cannons, anchors and other objects. Over the following years, archaeologists from the state of North Carolina studied the site. In 2011, after careful research, the state officially confirmed that the wreck was the Queen Anne's Revenge. Historians and archaeologists consider it one of the most important pirate shipwrecks ever found. Even so, the identification depended on careful comparison of finds with historical records. Among the clues were the large number of cannons, French objects and a bell dated 1709, all consistent with Blackbeard's ship.

conservation-lab-cannon-concretion-tank-.head: Objects from the wreck are slowly cleaned and conserved in a laboratory in North Carolina.
conservation-lab-cannon-concretion-tank-.body: When objects lie on the seabed for centuries, they become covered with a hard crust of sand, shells and rust, called concretion. Large lumps of concretion often contain smaller objects hidden inside. Archaeologists recover these lumps and bring them to the conservation laboratory of the Queen Anne's Revenge project in Greenville, North Carolina. There, specialists carefully remove the crust, using X-rays to see what lies inside. Iron objects such as cannons must be soaked in special solutions for years to remove salt, which would otherwise destroy them. Historians note that this work is slow and expensive. More than thirty cannons have been recovered so far, together with anchors and hundreds of thousands of smaller objects. Even so, the work continues, and parts of the wreck still remain on the seabed. Each object adds a small detail to the picture of life aboard the ship, from weapons to cooking utensils and personal belongings.

museum-display-ship-bell-anchor-cannon-s.head: Finds from the Queen Anne's Revenge include gold dust, pewter plates, medical instruments and navigation tools.
museum-display-ship-bell-anchor-cannon-s.body: The wreck has produced a remarkable variety of objects. Archaeologists have found small amounts of gold dust and a few gold coins, possibly from West Africa. They have found pewter plates and cups, glass bottles, wine glasses and pottery. Medical items include the brass syringe and other instruments. Navigation tools include parts of instruments, sounding leads and weights. There are cannonballs, lead shot, pieces of weapons and the ship's bell. Many of these finds are displayed at the North Carolina Maritime Museum in Beaufort, close to where the ship was lost. Historians value these objects because they show the real material world of pirates, beyond the legends. Some items, such as French tableware, reflect the ship's earlier life as La Concorde. Even so, there is no great treasure. The finds tell the story of a working ship with a large crew. Visitors can see the bell, cannons and many smaller objects in quiet museum galleries.

ocracoke-village-harbour-lighthouse-whit.head: Today, Ocracoke is a quiet island village reached by ferry, with a lighthouse built in 1823.
ocracoke-village-harbour-lighthouse-whit.body: Ocracoke lies near the southern end of the Outer Banks of North Carolina. Most of the island is protected as part of the Cape Hatteras National Seashore. The island can be reached only by ferry or small aircraft. Ferries cross from Hatteras Island to the north and from the mainland across Pamlico Sound. The longer crossings take more than two hours. Pelicans often fly low beside the ferries, and dolphins can sometimes be seen. The small village surrounds a harbour called Silver Lake, lined with boats and houses. The white Ocracoke Lighthouse, built in 1823, is one of the oldest operating lighthouses in the United States. Historians note that the island remained isolated for most of its history, and its residents developed a distinctive local dialect. Even so, Ocracoke is now a popular destination for visitors. In the evenings, the harbour is calm, and the light from the lighthouse shines over the sound.

empty-wide-beach-dunes-sea-oats-atlantic.head: The wild ponies of Ocracoke have lived on the island for centuries and are cared for by the National Park Service.
empty-wide-beach-dunes-sea-oats-atlantic.body: Ocracoke is known for its wild ponies, small and sturdy horses that have lived on the island for centuries. Their origins are uncertain. According to tradition, they descend from Spanish horses brought ashore from shipwrecks or early expeditions in the sixteenth or seventeenth centuries. Genetic studies suggest Spanish ancestry. Historians note that horses roamed freely on the Outer Banks for generations, grazing on marsh grass. In the twentieth century, as roads and traffic increased, the ponies were moved into a large fenced pasture for their safety. Since 1959, they have been cared for by the National Park Service. Visitors can see them from a viewing platform. Beyond the village, long beaches stretch along the Atlantic, backed by dunes covered with sea oats. Even so, the island remains vulnerable to storms and rising seas. Hurricanes have flooded the village several times in recent decades, and residents work hard to protect their community.

sound-side-marsh-grass-still-water-chann.head: Teach's Hole, where Blackbeard anchored, is still a channel near the southern tip of Ocracoke.
sound-side-marsh-grass-still-water-chann.body: On the sound side of Ocracoke, near the southern tip of the island, lies a deeper channel in the shallow water. It is called Teach's Hole, after Blackbeard, whose name was sometimes spelled Teach. According to tradition, this is where he anchored before his final battle in 1718. The area is surrounded by marsh grass and quiet water. Historians note that the channel has changed shape over three centuries, but the name has survived. In the village, a small shop and exhibition tell the story of Blackbeard and the pirates. Every year in autumn, Ocracoke holds a pirate festival with costumes, music and storytelling. Local legends say that on dark nights, a light can sometimes be seen moving over the water at Teach's Hole. Even so, such stories belong to folklore rather than history. They show how deeply the memory of Blackbeard has become part of the island's identity, more than three hundred years after his death.

ferry-crossing-calm-sound-pelicans-golde.head: Blackbeard's story is preserved today in archives, museums and the landscapes where he sailed.
ferry-crossing-calm-sound-pelicans-golde.body: More than three hundred years after his death, Blackbeard remains the best-known pirate in history. His story can be followed through many places: Nassau in the Bahamas, Charleston in South Carolina, Bath and Ocracoke in North Carolina, and Williamsburg in Virginia. Letters, trial records and ship logs in archives in London, Paris and the American states record his actions. The wreck of the Queen Anne's Revenge has added physical evidence, from cannons to cups and coins. Historians continue to study his life, and new research still changes how he is understood. Even so, much remains uncertain, including his origins and many details of his career. The legend and the history continue to exist side by side. In the evening, ferries cross the wide, calm sounds of the Outer Banks. Pelicans fly low over the water, and the low islands lie quietly under a golden sky, as they did in the autumn of 1718.
